https://www.dw.com/en/china-dozens-dead-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I92O Gansu Province's Danghe River saw water levels rise rapidly amid the rainfall Image: Lang Bingbing/Xinhua/picture alliance Advertisement The death toll after a flash flood in the northern Gansu province of China has climbed to 25, according to state media reports. The flood has left 23 others injured, the ⁠official Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday. What do we know about the Gansu flash floods? The Shuangshimen Scenic Area, a popular tourist spot for camping, was hit by a flash flood on July 26, with state media initially reporting 10 deaths and 23 injuries. The country's national commission for disaster prevention said it would oversee an investigation into the event. Videos of the flood show a deluge ripping through a valley where several tents and cars were parked. China has been hit by extreme weather this summer, with flooding affecting various areas in the country Image: Lang Bingbing/Xinhua/IMAGO Authorities have warned of further landslides, including in ‌Dingxi, ​as heavy downpour continues in the annual flood season. Beijing and Inner Mongolia also issued weather warnings on Sunday as China's ​weather observatory warned of heavy rain, high winds and thunderstorms across a large stretch of the country from ⁠the southwest ​to the northeast. Gen. Kevin D. Admiral, commanding general of III Armored Corps, speaks at a welcoming ceremony at Fort Hood, Texas, July 10, 2026. Admiral was nominated this week to serve as the next leader of U.S. Army Europe and Africa. (Anthony Heatley/U.S. Army) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published July 24, 2026 · STUTTGART, Germany — Lt. Gen. Kevin D. Admiral was nominated this week to serve as the next leader of U.S. Army Europe and Africa. Admiral, whose nomination was announced Thursday by the Pentagon, would also serve as the leader of NATO land forces in Europe. He currently serves as the commander of III Corps and Fort Hood in Texas. The nomination called for Admiral’s reappointment to the rank of lieutenant general in line with the Pentagon’s decision to downgrade USAREUR-AF’s headquarters to a three-star command . Prior to leading III Corps, Admiral served as the Army’s director of force management and before that commanded the 3rd Cavalry Regiment. The Army’s mission in Europe has been in transition since the departure of Gen. Christopher Donahue , who relinquished command earlier this month. Widely regarded as one of the Army’s most innovative leaders, Donahue put in his retirement papers in June. His exit became a point of contention, with backers saying he was forced into retirement by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The Defense Department never publicly addressed the circumstances surrounding Donahue’s retirement. If confirmed, Admiral will come to the job with experience commanding at numerous levels. He also will lead at a time when the Army’s mission in Europe is adapting as the Pentagon adjusts force levels on the Continent. Among the recent moves was the Pentagon’s decision to cancel the deployment of a Fort Hood-based armored brigade to Poland. At the same time, the Pentagon and Polish leaders have been in talks about increasing U.S. troop presence in that country in other ways. Meanwhile, the Pentagon has said it will reduce its troop presence in Germany by about 5,000, but it hasn’t fully detailed how that will be accomplished. Army Europe John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa. Based in Stuttgart, Germany, he previously worked for newspapers in New Jersey, North Carolina and Maryland. He is a graduate of the University of Delaware. https://www.dw.com/en/us-wildfire-forces.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JIFk Thousands have been forced to evacuate as the wildfire spreads Image: Trevor Bexon/Getty Images/AFP Advertisement A fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes near Reno in the US state of Nevada over the weekend. An unknown number of homes have been destroyed and at least six people have been injured. Officials have expanded the "GO NOW" zone to include almost 90,000 residents as conditions make the fire unpredicatable. What do we know about the Hawk Fire in Nevada? The fire started Saturday morning off Hawk Meadow Trail and spread rapidly through the Peavine Peak area northwest of the city, growing to between roughly 13,000 and 15,000 acres by Sunday. About 42,000 residents were ordered to evacuate, with another 45,000 told to be ready to leave, officials said. The evacuation zone stretched to the edge of the University of Nevada in northwest Reno, a city of more than 280,000 people near the California border. At least six people were injured — three first responders and three civilians — local authorities said. Officials said the fire was human-caused but have not released further details. "The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas," fire chief Richard Edwards told AFP. Officials say the Hawk Fire was human-caused Image: Trevor Bexon/Getty Images/AFP Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the National Guard, deploying two helicopters and 60 troops to assist firefighting and security efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said, according to Reuters. Human cost of the wildfire The fire has already destroyed homes. Cari Kieffer told AP her family fled with only minutes to spare, grabbing clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes, but leaving behind birth certificates and childhood photos. "I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," she said. "I was like, we gotta go like now." "We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone." Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from about 60,000 the day before, AP reported. Parts of US Route 395 were closed, two hospitals evacuated patients, and officials monitored whether the county jail would need to be evacuated. The Reno-Tahoe airport remained outside the evacuation zone, with flights operating normally. The blaze adds to a wave of fire activity across the drought-stricken Western United States this year. Fifteen new fires broke out across Nevada on Saturday alone. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/21/vene.text: A Venezuelan national was shot and wounded by a US immigration agent, Texas officials said on Sunday, as they voiced outrage and demanded a thorough investigation.Tasked with enforcing Trump's immigration crackdown, heavily armed and often masked US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have faced nationwide backlash for aggressive and often violent tactics, including the shooting of American citizens.The man, identified by his lawyer as 28-year-old Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was taken to a hospital in Texas's capital city Austin in a serious but stable condition after being shot in the torso, officials said.The wounded man's lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said on X that Garces Perez had been shot by an ICE agent while making "a DoorDash delivery."The shooting took place during a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in the Texas capital, Mayor Kirk Watson told a press conference.The Department of Homeland Security said Monday it was leading an investigation into the officer involved in the shooting with the help of the FBI.The department said in a post on X that the man had "illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal.""The illegal alien's condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal," it added.Watson said he was "very angry and extremely disappointed that a person was shot on the streets of Austin by ICE."He said local law enforcement should be involved in the investigation."The credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate," he said.Texas Democratic Representative Greg Casar echoed that sentiment, telling reporters that "ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities."Casar cited the January shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis in which video footage belied ICE accounts that she had attempted to run over a federal agent."It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," he said. "A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come...I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot."The House Democrat called for the release of body camera footage of Sunday's incident.Deportation threatA few hours later, Casar said Garces Perez had been "taken out of the hospital and into ICE custody.""If ICE deports him, the key witness to their shooting disappears," the lawmaker added. "He must not be removed from this country and he must receive proper medical care."Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was placed "into custody, but we still don't know his location."The shooting sparked outrage in the community with video footage posted by local news outlets to social media showing several dozen people protesting at the alleged shooting site.Donald Trump campaigned for president in 2016 and again in 2024, on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants, and has taken a series of dramatic actions since returning to the White House aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.Nearly 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the United States in August, according to Department of Homeland Security figures.Ruben Ray Martinez, a 23-year-old was shot by ICE in March 2025, in what the Texas Tribune said was the first known killing by immigration agents of an American in Trump's second term.
